Learning Objectives
Recognize the clinical symptoms of degenerative cervical myelopathy.
Assess the early and late clinical signs consistent with degenerative cervical myelopathy.
Interpret results of various imaging techniques in the evaluation of degenerative cervical
myelopathy.
List the main subtypes of degenerative cervical myelopathy.
Determine indications for and outcomes of nonsurgical and surgical management for
degenerative cervical myelopathy.
Apply clinical practice guidelines for the management of degenerative cervical myelopathy.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview

Cervical myelopathy describes a constellation of symptoms and signs arising from spinal cord
compression at the level of the spinal cord.
Early clinical manifestations are subtle but are important to detect.
Cord compression causes myelopathy via direct mechanical effect on cord function and/or an
ischemic effect secondary to compression of the anterior spinal artery.
The natural history of cervical myelopathy typically includes stable periods punctuated by
unpredictable stepwise progression.
Early management before the onset of irreversible spinal cord damage is essential for optimal
outcomes.

Overview
Cervical degeneration is second only to low back pain in causing symptomatic spinal
pathology; however, radiographic evidence of cervical degeneration is commonly
observed in asymptomatic adult patients (Resource 1). The constellation of degenerative
cervical changes associated with spinal cord dysfunction is known as degenerative
cervical myelopathy (DCM). DCM is the most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction
and results from stenosis of the cervical canal secondary to cervical spondylosis or
ligamentous irregularities. These changes include facet joint hypertrophy, ossification of
the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL), and ligamentum flavum hypertrophy and
ossification, which result from age-related changes and from repetitive injury caused by
developing instability.
Epidemiology
70% of patients aged 65 years or older have radiographic evidence of cervical degeneration.
Symptoms of spinal cord compression occur in 25% of these patients.

Epidemiology
DCM is increasing in prevalence because of the aging population. More than 70% of the
population aged1 65 years or older exhibit radiographic evidence of cervical

9/3/26, 7:38 AM

2/39

degeneration, with symptoms related to cord compression occurring in approximately
25% of these patients.2 In North America, the estimated incidence of DCM is 41 per
million persons per year, with an estimated prevalence of 605 per million and
approximately 7.88 persons per 100,000 requiring hospitalization each year. Because of
varied terminology used and the low number of epidemiologic investigations conducted,
these figures likely are underestimated.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
Aging causes degeneration of the intervertebral disks.
Disk degeneration leads to end plate stress.
End plate stress leads to instability with facet and ligament hypertrophy.

Osteology
The normal aging process causes biomechanical and biochemical changes in the
vertebral column, culminating in anatomic changes. The degeneration starts in the disks,
which degenerate and fail in their load-bearing function. This leads to increased stress
on the cartilage end plates, which causes subsequent synovial inflammation, narrowing
of the joint space, facet joint hypertrophy, and cervical kyphosis. In response,
osteophytes form and the ligamentum flavum hypertrophies to bring stability to the
spine. Pathologic changes that occur in the cervical spinal column and the spinal cord in
patients with DCM are shown in Figure 1.

Nerves
Disruption of the microvasculature causes ischemia, which leads to failure of the blood-cord
barrier and neuroinflammation.
These in turn lead to cytologic changes in the cord.
These changes cause apoptosis of neurons, which results in symptomatic myelopathy.

Nerves
DCM leads to irreversible cytologic and histologic damage through changes in the
microvascular supply to the cord, ischemia, disruption of the blood-cord barrier,
neuroinflammation, and dendrocytic and neuronal apoptosis (Resource 2).
Natural History
The natural history of DCM is not completely understood because of the limited numbers of
longitudinal studies.
DCM typically progresses in a stepwise manner; however, the pathology progresses linearly.
Function decreases by one point on the modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA)
scale over 6 years in 60% of patients.

Natural History
The natural history of DCM is difficult to establish because of the paucity of longitudinal
studies. Early reports on cervical myelopathy suggested that the condition was
characterized by long periods of stability with a stepwise deterioration; however the
pathologic changes observed in patients with DCM are being increasingly recognized as
linearly progressive. The most common symptom observed early in the development of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:38 AM
AAOS | Cervical Myelopathy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002023
5/39

symptomatic myelopathy is widening of the gait, with other upper motor neuron
symptoms and functional impairment following. Clinically, 60% of patients with
symptomatic DCM deteriorate by one point on the mJOA score within 6 years of initial
assessment.3
Risk Factors
Genetic, occupational, and medical risk factors for DCM.
Most genetic and occupational risks are not fully understood.
Congenital cervical stenosis has a clear association with DCM and should be identified in
assessing a patient.

Risk Factors
Smoking, diabetes mellitus, obesity, movement disorders, hypoparathyroidism, and
hypophosphatemic rickets are associated with an increased risk of DCM. Porters, pilots
engaged in maneuvers, and individuals who participate in contact sports also have a
higher risk of accelerated cervical degeneration. Interestingly, no evidence suggests that
motor vehicle collisions lead to DCM.
Evidence suggests that a genetic predisposition to DCM exists; however, despite the high
prevalence of the disease, the evidence supporting the individual loci is poor. Most
suspected genes are responsible for bone physiology or collagen metabolism; however,
additional studies are necessary to characterize these. An important cohort vulnerable
to DCM is the East Asian population, who have an increased risk of OPLL and ossification
of the ligamentum flavum compared with other populations.
Congenital cervical stenosis is a substantial risk factor for DCM. Congenital cervical
stenosis is defined as a sagittal canal diameter less than 13 mm or a Torg-Pavlov ratio
less than 0.8; the reduction in space available for the cord means that even small
intrusions may give rise to the pathologic cascade. Similarly, patients with hypermobility
syndromes, such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, have excessive laxity of their ligaments,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:38 AM
AAOS | Cervical Myelopathy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002023
6/39

leading to cervical instability with consequent accelerated degeneration of the
supporting structures, joint pain, and atlantoaxial instability. Patients with Down
syndrome have cervical instability, odontoid dysmorphology, and C1 hypoplasia, which
may indirectly lead to DCM.
Some less well-defined associations with DCM exist, including schizophrenia and
Parkinson disease, in which disordered movement leads to cervical dystonia and
abnormal posture. Klippel-Feil syndrome results in congenital fusion of C2 and C3,
leading to an increased risk of cervical facet degeneration and consequent DCM. Patients
with cerebral palsy, torticollis, and Tourette syndrome have a propensity for early
degenerative cervical changes.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Clinical Presentation
Upper extremity symptoms
Generalized feeling of clumsiness of the arms and hands; patient reports dropping things
Loss of dexterity with an inability to manipulate fine objects, such as buttons, and trouble
with handwriting
Diffuse (typically nondermatomal) numbness
Lower extremity symptoms
Gait instability, imbalance, dysesthesia, and inability to tandem gait
Lhermitte phenomenon: electric shock–like sensations that radiate down the spine or trunk
or into the extremities with flexion of the neck
Other potential symptoms
Subjective weakness
Bowel and bladder (sphincter) dysfunction
Loss of motor strength
Axial neck pain
Patient History


Patient History
If DCM is suspected, a careful patient history will reveal a constellation of symptoms that
include axial, upper, and lower limb symptoms. Common symptoms include neck pain or
stiffness, weakness or numbness in any of the four limbs, and loss of dexterity (eg,
inability to button a shirt or difficulty writing). A classic early symptom is an ataxic gait.
Patients report a widening of their base when walking, with imbalance, stumbling, and
falls, and an inability to tandem walk.
The timeline of progression is important to define. More rapid progression is suggestive
of critical stenosis, whereas a more gradual decline is suggestive of earlier compression.
Physical Examination
Severe weakness of the major muscle groups in the upper or lower extremities is uncommon.
A loss of fine motor dexterity may be observed by asking patients to fasten a button or pick up
a pen. Patients may be unable to perform rapid opening and closing of the fingers.
Disordered proprioception (indicating dorsal column dysfunction) occurs with advanced
disease and is associated with a poor prognosis.
Gait assessment is critical. Patients may demonstrate a wide-based gait, ataxia, slow speed,
shortened stride lengths, and an inability to perform tandem gait.
Hyperreflexia may be present in patients with myelopathy. Hyperreflexia should be considered
if more than five repeated percussions of a deep tendon stimulate a corresponding motor
response each time.
Hoffman reflex is the most common finding, being present in 80% of myelopathic patients.
Patients with concomitant peripheral nerve dysfunction from conditions such as diabetes
mellitus, hypothyroidism, peripheral neuropathy, and severe multilevel cervical foraminal
stenosis may have diminished or absent reflexes, which may mislead the examiner.
Patients with cervical myelopathy who have coexisting lumbar stenosis may exhibit brisk
upper extremity reflexes consistent with upper motor neuron findings yet diminished lower
extremity reflexes because of the root level compression in the lumbar spine.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:38 AM


Physical Examination
A complete neurologic examination should be performed in every patient in whom DCM
is suspected because it may expose a series of specific findings.1 The earliest sign
evident in patients with DCM is widening of the base when walking, occasionally with
accompanying ataxia. Other key findings to uncover include the Hoffman reflex, in which
passive rapid flexion (a flicking maneuver) of the distal interphalangeal joint of the ring
finger causes flexion of the ipsilateral thumb interphalangeal joint; and the Trömner
sign, demonstrated by flexion of the thumb and index finger in response to tapping the
volar surface of the distal phalanx of the middle finger, which is held partly flexed
between the examiner’s finger and thumb.
An inverted radial reflex is detected in some patients with myelopathy. With this sign, the
fingers flex as the radial side of the wrist is tapped rather than the normal finding of
elbow flexion and wrist radial deviation. Also visible in patients with myelopathy is the
Babinski sign, which consists of great toe extension and fanning of the other toes in
response to stroking the plantar surface of the foot.
The Lhermitte phenomenon may be observed in some patients. In these patients, flexion
of the neck gives rise to electric shock sensations radiating down the spine; limbs; and,
occasionally, the trunk.
If very severe, myelopathy may cause spasticity in the limbs and muscle atrophy. These
findings may be subtle but are important to distinguish to characterize the severity of
the disease and the potential for recovery after management.
Assessing the Severity of DCM
The mJOA scale can be reliably used to assess the severity and progression of DCM (Table 1).
Other grading systems include the Neck Disability Index , the Nurick Grading System, and the
visual analog scale.

Assessing the Severity of DCM
Classification systems are useful in patients with DCM to detect progression of disease
and assess the resolution of symptoms after management.
The mJOA scale was designed in the 1990s to classify cervical myelopathy. Scored from 0
to 18, with lower scores representing poorer function, it classifies patients as having
severe (<12), moderate (12 to 14), or mild (>14) cervical myelopathy. The score assesses
hand function, walking, and sphincter dysfunction to determine severity. The scale is
associated with high interobserver reliability and an ability to detect clinically important
change2 (Table 1).
The Neck Disability Index was developed in 1991 to assess the effect of neck pain on a
patient’s activities of daily living. A higher score represents poorer function, and the
clinically important difference is 5 points. The Neck Disability Index is useful in identifying
improvement in function after surgical management of DCM (Resource 3).
The Nurick Grading System assesses gait impairment in patients diagnosed with DCM. It
is clinician-based and consists of six grades of DCM, ranging from 0 to 5, with higher
scores representing poorer function3 (Table 2).

Moderate evidence shows that mJOA scale scores improve postoperatively by more than
a minimal clinically important difference. Therefore, the mJOA scale has been adopted as
the standard for evaluating functional impairment in patients with DCM, especially in
patients with moderate and severe myelopathy. Less robust evidence shows that Nurick
Grading System scores improve, perhaps because the fewer number of categories make
the scale less sensitive. In addition to the mJOA scale and Nurick Grading System, many
clinicians use the visual analog scale for pain or disability indices, such as the Medical
Outcomes Study 36-Item Short Form (SF-36), to determine a patient’s function and
improvement.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Useful to define cervical alignment and instability
Used to measure cervical sagittal vertical axis, assessment of C2-C7 global sagittal alignment,
and T1 slope


Radiography
Plain radiography continues to have a role in investigating cervical myelopathy,
demonstrating degeneration of disks and facet joints, bony stenosis of the spinal canal,
and overall cervical alignment. Plain flexion and extension lateral radiographs are used
to assess the dynamic stability of the cervical spine, with instability influencing treatment
options offered to patients.
Plain lateral radiographs can be used to assess overall cervical sagittal alignment. The
cervical sagittal vertical axis measures the horizontal distance between a plumb line
drawn from C2 and the posterosuperior corner of the C7 vertebral body and describes
the sagittal imbalance of the cervical spine. The C2-C7 global sagittal alignment
measures the Cobb angle subtended by the inferior end plate of C2 and the inferior end
plate of C7 to define overall cervical lordosis or kyphosis. The T1 slope is an assessment
of the overall sagittal alignment of the spine as a function of the spinopelvic parameters.
The sagittal balance of the cervical spine is affected by the size and orientation of the T1
slope, with a difference between the T1 slope and C2-C7 global sagittal alignment
exceeding 17° indicating cervical deformity, which should be managed during fusion1
(Table 3).

Another useful measurement to assess on plain lateral radiographs is the Torg-Pavlov
ratio. First defined in 1987, this measurement describes the space available for the
spinal cord at a given level. It is calculated by dividing the width of the spinal canal by the

14/39

width of the vertebral body at a given level. A value less than 0.8 indicates potentially
substantial congenital cervical stenosis, which should be considered during evaluation
and treatment planning.
Computed Tomography
Unenhanced CT is useful in defining bony anatomy and planning instrumentation
preoperatively.
CT myelography is less commonly performed; however, it has a role in patients with OPLL.

Computed Tomography
Plain CT is useful in defining bony anatomy at a higher resolution than that available via
plain radiography. It also may contribute to diagnosis if MRI is not possible, such as in
patients with an MRI-incompatible pacemaker or patients with other contraindications to
MRI. CT myelography is an invasive variation of standard CT in which the subdural space
is infiltrated with contrast before the patient is mobilized and scanned to identify areas
of thecal impingement. Although it may be technically difficult and challenging to
perform and interpret, CT myelography has a role in assessing patients who are not
suitable candidates for MRI. CT myelography also may aid in diagnosing OPLL, which
may not be obvious on MRI or plain radiographs, and may guide surgical approach and
planning.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI typically is the most informative imaging modality in evaluating DCM.
Signal change (myelomalacia) within the cord, most visible on T2-weighted images, suggests
severe cord compression.
The modified K-line may aid in assessing cervical sagittal alignment and making decisions
regarding surgical approach.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:38 AM
AAOS | Cervical Myelopathy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002023
15/39


Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI can define the anatomy of spinal cord compression in most patients with DCM and
is useful to exclude other causes of cord dysfunction, such as tumor or syringomyelia.
Unenhanced MRI can show spondylolysis, OPLL, ligamentum flavum hypertrophy, and
disk bulges or herniation; however, MRI may be inadequate with respect to showing the
full extent of OPLL in some patients.
Sagittal MRIs are useful in determining the ratio of the smallest cord diameter to the
largest transverse cord diameter at the same level, which is known as the compression
ratio. A ratio less than 0.4 is associated with poor prognosis, whereas a value exceeding
0.4 correlates with recovery.
A useful measurement to help guide treatment decisions is the modified K-line, which
was defined in 2013. It is a measurement that combines the effect of a kyphotic cervical
spine and anterior compressive elements and OPLL. The line is described by a line
joining the midpoint of the spinal cord at C2 and the midpoint of the cord at C7 on a T1-
weighted midsagittal MRI. Once drawn, the distance between the line and any anterior
compressive factors, such as disks or osteophytes, is measured. If the anterior
compressive pathology lies within 4 mm or crosses the K-line (K-line –), posterior
decompression alone likely will be insufficient to fully decompress the cord regardless of
restoration of lordosis and indicates that anterior decompression may be necessary. If
the modified K-line is more than 4 mm from the anterior compressive pathology (K-line
+), posterior decompression alone may be sufficient (Figure 2).

Consecutive MRI sequences may help define the degree of cord scarring and damage,
which, if visible on images, constitutes myelomalacia. Signal change is caused by
cavitation or cord necrosis, both of which are closely correlated with poor outcomes.
Hypointense areas within the cord on T1-weighted images and intramedullary
hyperintensity on T2-weighted images are associated with worse clinical neurologic
symptoms and more permanent deficits.
As MRI techniques have progressed, the microstructure of the cord has become better
visualized and evaluated. Quantitative microstructural MRI can measure the cross-

sectional area of lesions and ratio of white to gray matter, which may aid in assessing the
progression of myelopathy before clinical signs are detected.
Other Studies
Neurophysiologic studies aid in diagnosis and help exclude coexistent cervical radiculopathy
and neuromuscular disease.
Nerve conduction studies are performed in patients in whom polyneuropathy, nerve
entrapment, or plexopathy must be excluded.

Other Studies
Neurophysiologic testing has been advocated by some studies in the routine
investigation of DCM; however, it is particularly useful in detecting subclinical pathology
and identifying patients who would benefit from close monitoring. Electromyography is
an invasive technique that is used to detect injury to the anterior horn cells, which are
most at risk in patients with compressive DCM. If DCM is present, electromyography will
demonstrate high amplitude, long duration polyphasic potentials, and reduced motor
unit recruitment. Active denervation is suggested by fibrillation action potentials and
positive sharp waves. Latency and low-amplitude signals observed in somatosensory-
evoked potentials suggest conduction impairment in DCM. Similarly, latency in motor-
evoked potentials is useful to detect conduction compromise.
In most patients, intraoperative neurophysiologic monitoring should be used during the
surgical management of DCM to identify impending neurologic compromise and prevent
neurologic consequences. In patients with severe spinal stenosis and DCM, awake
intubation and prepositioning intraoperative neurophysiologic monitoring should be
considered.
Pathology
Compression of the cord leads to direct neural dysfunction.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:38 AM
AAOS | Cervical Myelopathy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002023
18/39

The microvascular supply is compromised, leading to ischemia and blood-cord barrier
disruption, followed by neuroinflammation.
The terminal event is cellular apoptosis and cord dysfunction.
Dynamic and static compression may be present.

Pathology
Dysfunction of the cord from cervical degeneration is caused by several mechanisms.
First, the mechanical forces applied by anatomic changes—disk bulges, anterior
osteophytes, OPLL, facet joint hypertrophy, and ossification of the ligamentum flavum—
cause direct injury to the neuronal cells and their supporting glial cells, which
compromises cord physiology and function. Impaired cord perfusion caused by
compression of the anterior spinal artery, vertebral arteries, and radicular arteries leads
to cord ischemia. This is exacerbated by increased cord tortuosity and pathologic
changes to the vessel walls, at which thickening and hyalinization occur.1 As myelopathy
progresses, the blood-cord barrier is compromised via loss of endothelial cells through
hypoxic cell death.
Inflammation plays a key role in the development of cord dysfunction. Increased
vascular permeability with associated edema and inflammatory cell infiltration cause the
activation of microglia and macrophages, which leads to neuronal injury and apoptosis.
The histologic characteristics of DCM involve demyelination, cavitation, gliosis, and gray
and white matter degeneration, with accompanying wallerian degeneration of the
ascending and descending tracts. Early in the development of DCM, loss of axons within
the lateral corticospinal tracts is identified, which reflects the culmination of the
pathophysiology.
In addition to the aforementioned factors that function via static compression, cord
compression may result from dynamic mechanisms, such as minor trauma of
degenerative spondylolisthesis and instability contributing to compression. Patients with
more than 3 mm of dynamic spondylolisthesis may be at risk of dynamic cord
compression. Patients with cervical stenosis have a higher risk for cervical cord injury
after minor neck trauma, particularly if the cervical spine is forced into extension,

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002023
19/39

reducing the interval between the anterior osteophytes and the posterior longitudinal
ligament and the hypertrophied ligamentum flavum (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Flowchart shows the pathophysiologic process of degenerative cervical
myelopathy. Static factors (eg, spondylosis, ligament hypertrophy, calcification) reduce
the cross-sectional area of the spinal canal. This effect is exacerbated by dynamic factors
during pathologic movement (eg, degenerative subluxation) and physiologic movement.
Consequent chronic spinal cord compression results in ischemia owing to regional
malperfusion and local vessel deformation. Chronic compression also disrupts the
blood–spinal cord barrier (BSCB) via endothelial cell dysfunction and hypoxic cell death
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:38 AM
AAOS | Cervical Myelopathy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002023
20/39

as a result of ischaemia. BSCB disruption permits entry of peripheral inflammatory cells
into the spinal cord parenchyma. Activation of microglia and recruitment of
macrophages follows; these processes also may be triggered via the CX3CR1–CX3CL1
axis secondary to ischemia. The ensuing neuroinflammatory process and ischemia
activate apoptotic pathways, culminating in neuronal and oligodendroglial cell death.
HLF = hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum, OPLL = ossification of the posterior
longitudinal ligament. (Reproduced with permission from Badhiwala JH, Ahuja CS, Akbar
MA, et al: Degenerative cervical myelopathy: Update and future directions. Nat Rev
Neurol 2020;16[2]:108-124.)
OPLL and Ossification of the Ligamentum Flavum
Overview and epidemiology
OPLL and ossification of the ligamentum flavum are potential causes of cervical myelopathy
from anterior and posterior compression, respectively.
Both pathologies are most common in the East Asian population.

OPLL and Ossification of the Ligamentum Flavum
The causes of OPLL and ossification of the ligamentum flavum remain unclear; however,
they are most likely multifactorial, with genetic, hormonal, and environmental
influences. Risk factors include East Asian ethnicity, diabetes mellitus, obesity, a high-salt
and low-meat diet, poor calcium absorption, and mechanical stress on the posterior
longitudinal ligament. The same general guidelines that apply to selection of approach in
patients with other causes of DCM apply to the management of OPLL and ossification of
the ligamentum flavum. In patients with severe OPLL, a posterior approach may be
preferable and safer, irrespective of the number of stenotic levels involved.
Differential Diagnosis
Less common causes of cervical cord compression (eg, epidural abscess, tumor, trauma) may
result in cervical myelopathy. These patients usually present somewhat differently, with pain,

Kyphosis (primary or postlaminectomy)
A broad differential diagnosis should be considered, including nonspinal disorders, such as
stroke, movement disorders, neuromuscular disorders, brachial plexopathy/neuritis, and
multiple sclerosis.
Management
Surgical treatment is recommended for patients with moderate to severe DCM (Resource 4).
Surgical treatment is an option in patients with mild DCM who are symptomatic, have pain, or
demonstrate deterioration in their quality of life.
Surgical management may improve functional outcomes, pain, and neurologic status.
Early intervention, before permanent changes occur in the spinal cord, improves the
prognosis.
If nonsurgical treatment is elected in patients with mild DCM, careful and frequent follow-up is
mandatory. Orthoses, anti-inflammatory medications, analgesic agents, and isometric
exercises may be considered.
Patients without myelopathy who have cord compression and symptoms or electrophysiologic
evidence of radiculopathy have a higher risk of myelopathy and cord injury, which may favor
the decision to proceed with surgical treatment.
Nonsurgical Management
Indications

Indications
Although nonsurgical management does not appear to cause a deterioration in
symptoms, little evidence suggests that it reverses or halts the progression of DCM in
patients with myelopathy. Options for nonsurgical management include cervical traction,
bracing, analgesia, physiotherapy-guided exercise, manual therapy, bed rest, and activity
modifications. Weak evidence supports the nonsurgical treatment of patients with mild
DCM; however, nonsurgical treatment is recommended in combination with close
observation in patients with DCM caused by a soft disk herniation.3 Each patient’s

preferences must be considered because patients without symptoms or slow
progression may be reluctant to undergo surgical treatment.
In patients with no symptoms of myelopathy in whom radiographic changes suggest a
risk for later development of myelopathy, regular review via MRI should be considered to
evaluate for progression of cervical stenosis and compressive pathology. This is
particularly important in patients with symptoms or electrophysiologic evidence of
radiculopathy, which is associated with a higher risk of progression to myelopathy. The
evidence supporting nonsurgical management is poor at best, and guidelines published
in 2017 suggest that surgical treatment or structured nonsurgical treatment are
reasonable in patients with mild myelopathy.
For patients with no signs of myelopathy and no radicular symptoms in whom signs of
compression are observed on MRI, regular follow-up with counseling regarding the signs
and symptoms to be watchful for is recommended. Clinically relevant disease will occur
in only 22.6% of such patients (Resource 5).
Studies have shown that the nonsurgical treatment of patients with single-level DCM
who have cord signal changes and an initial mJOA score1 of 13 leads to equivalent
outcomes; however, the evidence is not robust. This is countered by the higher incidence
of hospitalization because of cord injury in patients initially treated nonsurgically (13.9
per 1,000 person years) compared with patients treated surgically (9.4 per 1,000 person
years).
As many as 54% of patients will ultimately undergo surgical treatment, and earlier
surgical treatment should be considered in patients with:
Circumferential cord compression
Angular edged compression
Greater preoperative cervical range of movement
Lower lordosis at the site of compression
Greater spondylolisthesis (if present)
Segmental instability
Reduced cerebrospinal fluid diameter

Surgical Management

Surgical Management
Surgical treatment is offered to most patients with clinically evident DCM. Evidence
suggests that surgical management leads to improvement in functional scores and visual
analog scale scores for pain at all time points despite the traditional opinion that surgical
management can only halt the progression of symptoms (Resource 6). The greatest
improvements are observed in patients with moderate or severe DCM; therefore,
surgical treatment is recommended in these patients.
The primary goal of surgical management is to alleviate the mechanical compression on
the spinal cord. Successfully achieving this goal without creating iatrogenic instability or
deformity necessitates fusion to stabilize the vertebral column in most patients. Fusion
can be performed via an anterior, posterior, or combined approach. Although
considerable debate exists regarding the optimal surgical approach, evidence suggests
that the approaches yield similar improvements in neurologic status. No single
procedure is clearly superior in every situation; however, the following considerations
may favor one approach over another:
Number of stenotic levels present
Patient comorbidities
Desire to limit or preserve motion
Anterior approaches typically are used in patients with a loss of cervical lordosis and a
clear anterior-based pathology over two levels or fewer, because interbody fusion is an
opportunity to re-create this alignment, or if compression spans fewer levels. Anterior
procedures consist of:

Anterior cervical diskectomy and fusion
Anterior cervical corpectomy
Combined anterior cervical diskectomy and corpectomy
An important consideration in performing revision procedures via an anterior approach
is to preoperatively evaluate symmetric, bilateral vocal cord function via direct
laryngoscopy in consultation with an otolaryngologist. If asymmetric vocal cord function
is present, indicating a prior recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, then the approach should
be made via the same side. This is done to avoid bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve
injury, which may lead to bilateral vocal cord paralysis, dysphonia, and airway
compromise.
Posterior approaches are primarily used in patients in whom multilevel compression is
evident or in patients with primary posterior pathology, such as hypertrophied
ligamentum flavum. Posterior approaches also are considered in patients with OPLL and
evidence of preserved cervical lordosis, in whom loss of alignment is less likely. Posterior
surgical options include:
Posterior cervical laminectomy with instrumented fusion
Posterior cervical laminoplasty
Posterior uninstrumented laminectomy is performed rarely because of the risk of
subsequent kyphotic deformity.
Techniques/Procedures
Anterior cervical diskectomy and fusion (ACDF)
ACDF directly decompresses herniated disks, spondylotic bars, and OPLL.
The procedure contributes to the relief of spondylotic neck pain, addresses kyphosis,
immobilizes the segment of decompressed cord through interbody fusion, and prevents
recurrent disease over the fused segments.

For myelopathy arising from one or two disk spaces, single- or two-level ACDF is the
preferred treatment option for most patients. For patients with stenosis at three or more
disk segments, the superiority of an anterior approach is not as well defined.
Anterior corpectomy and fusion
Anterior corpectomy and fusion directly relieves neural compression resulting from kyphosis
by removing the vertebral bodies or posterior vertebral pathology over which the cord may
be draped.
The vacant segment is then grafted with a structural bone graft or an implant with cancellous
graft.
Corpectomies with long strut grafts are associated with good clinical results but require rigid
external immobilization if an anterior plate is not used. Graft harvest site morbidity may
compromise the overall outcome.
Supplemental posterior fixation and fusion may be required if two or more corpectomies are
performed to provide increased stability and reduce the incidence of graft kickout and
pseudarthrosis.
Graft dislodgment, reported to occur in as many as 20% of patients, may be associated with
neurologic compromise, esophageal injury, and airway obstruction.
A hybrid strategy in which corpectomy is combined with an ACDF provides increased
biomechanical stability compared with two-level corpectomy and may obviate the need for
posterior surgery.
The risks of complications may be higher in patients who undergo multilevel reconstruction
because of prolonged retraction and the extent of the exposure.
Surgical times exceeding 4 hours are associated with postoperative airway compromise.
Posterior laminectomy without fusion
This treatment option is not as preferable because long-term outcomes are less favorable
compared with laminectomy with fusion or laminoplasty.
Postlaminectomy kyphosis may occur after laminectomy, with rates ranging from 11% to
47%. Although this complication may result in recurrent myelopathy if the cord becomes
draped and compressed over the kyphosis, the incidence of clinically apparent neurologic
problems resulting from this complication is unclear.
Posterior laminectomy with fusion
This is effective in improving spondylotic neck pain and typically avoids postlaminectomy
kyphosis.
Any preexisting kyphosis can be improved after laminectomy by positioning the neck in
extension before securing the instrumentation. If kyphosis across a single motion segment

exceeds 11°, then an anterior approach in combination with posterior approach generally is

If fusion is not necessary, laminoplasty may be a better option if no evidence of deformity is

Posterior laminoplasty
Laminoplasty, a motion-preserving procedure that was initially proposed and performed in
Japan, has gained increased acceptance in North America. This technique achieves multilevel
posterior cord decompression while avoiding postlaminectomy kyphosis and preserving
motion.
Each variation of the technique expands the spinal canal, most often via the creation of a
hinge at the junction of the lateral mass and the lamina. The hinge is created by thinning the
dorsal cortex but not cutting through the ventral cortex completely, creating the hinge
through a greenstick fracture.
The unilateral osteotomy is held patent with bone, sutures, suture anchors, or specifically
designed plates.
A C3 through C7 procedure is performed in most patients.
Laminoplasty generally is a safer and technically easier procedure to perform than multilevel
anterior corpectomy, particularly in patients with severe stenosis or OPLL that requires
resection because indirect decompression is performed.
Laminoplasty does not preclude a later anterior procedure that may be required to manage
focal anterior compression.
Absence of lordosis is not an absolute contraindication to laminoplasty.
In patients with kyphosis who have compressive lesions arising posteriorly, laminoplasty also
may achieve direct decompression.
In patients with kyphosis and extremely tight cervical stenosis, laminoplasty may be
considered a first-stage procedure, with subsequent anterior surgery performed if necessary.
Combined anterior and posterior surgery
Combined anterior and posterior surgery is strongly recommended in patients with
substantial unreducible preoperative or postlaminectomy kyphosis.
Supplemental posterior fixation and fusion should be considered in patients with substantial
kyphosis requiring multilevel anterior corpectomies.
If multilevel corpectomy is performed to decompress the cord after previous laminectomy,
the right and left sides of the spine become disconnected from each other, creating an
extremely unstable biomechanical environment.

Complications
Surgical treatment typically is well tolerated by patients. The cumulative incidence of
complications is 14.1%.
Nonunion

Nonunion
Nonunion occurs infrequently if precise surgical technique is used and adequate bone
grafting is performed. The rate of pseudarthrosis is 1.8%.
Mortality

Mortality
The risk of mortality in patients who undergo elective surgical treatment for the
management of DCM is 0.3%. The rate of mortality is 0.33% with an anterior approach
and 0.69% with a posterior approach.
Pain

Pain
The management of postoperative pain should follow the same analgesic strategy as
that for other surgical procedures. After recovery from the immediate postoperative
period, the incidence of longer term axial pain is 5.6%. With longer term follow-up,
adjacent segment disease may become a problem in 1.5% of patients because of the
altered biomechanics of the cervical spine.

In patients with painful spondylosis, some evidence suggests laminoplasty should be
avoided because arthrodesis does not form part of the surgical strategy. If laminoplasty
is performed, controversy exists with regard to whether postoperative neck pain reflects
new-onset postoperative symptoms or is simply the persistence of preoperative
spondylotic pain.
Stiffness

Stiffness
In many patients, reducing the range of movement via arthrodesis is a deliberate effect
of surgical treatment. Preoperatively, many patients report reduced range of movement
that may be related to facet joint arthrosis with spontaneous stiffening. Cervical fusion is
thought to reduce subjective range of neck movement by as much as 50%, with
remaining movement coming from the occipitocervical junction or unfused segments.
Prolonged postoperative immobilization may contribute to long-term cervical stiffness,
which can be avoided by restricting immobilization to the short term, if at all.
Infection

Infection
Infection is rare in patients who undergo cervical surgery but may require surgical
management. The combined risk of superficial and deep infection requiring
management is 1.5%. The risk is higher with posterior cervical approaches than with
anterior cervical approaches.


Hardware Failure
The risk of hardware failure depends on understanding the alignment of the spine and
the biomechanics of the grafts and instrumentation to be used. The overall incidence of
graft or instrumentation failure is 2.0%.
Dural Tear

Dural Tear
Dural tears are a risk during any surgery to the vertebral column, and the risk increases
if the canal is entered. The cumulative risk of dural injury in patient who undergo surgical
treatment for the management of DCM is 1.4%.
Patients being treated for myelopathy resulting from OPLL often undergo an anterior
corpectomy. In these patients, the dura often is closely adherent to the ossified ligament
and may be difficult to separate while maintaining its integrity. Troublesome dural tears
can be avoided by allowing the adherent OPLL to float anteriorly after corpectomy
without removal.
Wound Healing

Wound Healing
Anterior cervical incisions rarely fail to heal given the excellent blood supply in the area.
Posteriorly, the effect of soft-tissue swelling and postoperative bleeding from the
paracervical musculature leads to a slightly increased risk of wound complications;
however, the overall risk of wound healing complications requiring management is 0.8%.

Hematoma

Hematoma
Hematoma is a specific risk that must be addressed during anterior and posterior
approaches because it may result in severe morbidity. With anterior approaches,
hematoma puts the airway at risk and may require urgent decompression, in some
patients outside the operating room. To mitigate this risk, a continuous suturing
technique is recommended for all layers during closure of an anterior cervical wound to
allow for rapid removal in an urgent situation, and the use of a drain is recommended
unless complete hemostasis is achieved. The incidence of hematoma after anterior
surgery is 0.8%.
With posterior approaches , hematoma may lead to compression of the cervical cord
after laminectomy. A surgical drain is recommended after posterior surgery to mitigate
the 2.12% risk of this complication.
The incidence of blood transfusion is low with anterior approaches because of the
absence of muscle division. Conversely, posterior approaches are associated with
considerable bleeding, leading to a 7.20% risk for required blood transfusion to maintain
a satisfactory hemoglobin count.
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy

Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Although neural injury is rare postoperatively, the cord is vulnerable to manipulation and
reperfusion injuries. The incidence of worsening myelopathy postoperatively is
approximately 1.3%, slightly exceeding the rate of nerve root injury of 0.9%. The C5
nerve root is at particular risk of palsy after decompression, the etiology of which is
unclear. Signs of C5 weakness occur in 1.9% of patients postoperatively; however, these
signs are temporary in most patients. Meticulous surgical technique should be used to

prevent this complication. Palsies tend to be motor dominant; however, sensory
dysfunction and radicular pain also may occur.
Palsy can occur at any time, from immediately postoperatively to 20 days
postoperatively, complicating what may otherwise appear to be successful spinal cord
decompression.
The peripheral nerves seldom are at risk during either approach to the spine, with the
notable exception of the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Classically thought to be more at risk
with a right-sided approach, evidence suggests that the risk of injury is the same
regardless of the laterality of the approach. However, the risk of injury is higher with
corpectomy than with diskectomy. Dysphonia has been identified in 0.7% of surgically
treated patients with DCM, with anterior approaches constituting most of these cases.
Dysphagia and esophageal injuries are more common complications, and most of these
complications occur during an anterior approach. Esophageal laceration rarely occurs,
with rates being 0.2%. Regardless, immediate identification of this complication is
required to prevent later systemic upset. Dysphagia occurs in 3.63% of patients who
undergo anterior surgery and 1.87% of patients who undergo posterior surgery,
suggesting an etiology of retraction and intubation.


Reperfusion
A degree of postoperative neurologic deterioration has been observed in as many as
11% of patients. This is thought to result from the molecular and cellular changes that
occur after decompression, and studies have shown that axonal plasticity underpins
functional recovery.1 Therefore, some pharmacologic agents have been used to
maximize recovery. One such agent is riluzole, a benzothiazole anticonvulsant that alters
excitatory neurotransmission. Early animal studies have suggested that this drug is

Other Complications
Revision surgery
The incidence of revision surgery from all causes is 1.4%.
Outcomes

Outcomes
Surgical treatment leads to substantial functional improvements in patients with short
and long duration of symptoms regardless of the severity of symptoms. Improvement is
less likely with a longer duration of symptoms and a higher preoperative mJOA score,
highlighting the importance of early diagnosis before irreversible tissue damage has
occurred. Patients who deteriorate in long-term follow-up should be evaluated for
adjacent segment degeneration in the cervical spine and other pathologies, including
lumbar spinal stenosis and hip or knee osteoarthritis.
